cards.q: Roots of the word pharmacovigilance
cards.a: Greek pharmacon (drug) plus Latin vigilare (keep watch)

cards.q: Threats a medicine-monitoring system guards against: list all
cards.a: Ineffective, substandard and counterfeit medicines

cards.q: WHO aims of pharmacovigilance programmes: list all
cards.a: Patient care and safety; public health and safety; detect and communicate problems; assess benefit and risk; safe, rational, cost-effective use; education and training

cards.q: Sarkar definition of adverse event
cards.a: Untoward medical occurrence during treatment, not necessarily caused by the drug

cards.q: Year sulfanilamide elixir made with diethylene glycol killed patients in USA
cards.a: 1937 (107 deaths)

cards.q: Year thalidomide was launched on the market
Year foetal abnormality reports from thalidomide appeared worldwide
cards.a: 1961 (most in Germany)

cards.q: Body set up in the UK in 1963 for drug safety monitoring
cards.a: British Committee on Safety of Drug Monitoring

cards.q: National ADR reporting systems started in 1964-65: list all
cards.a: UK, Australia, New Zealand, Canada, West Germany, Sweden

cards.q: Year WHO drug-monitoring centre moved from Geneva to Uppsala
cards.a: 1978 (Uppsala Monitoring Centre runs the programme)

cards.q: Drug whose withdrawal renewed interest in drug safety mechanisms
cards.a: Rofecoxib

cards.q: Other drugs that highlighted the need for effective PV: list all
cards.a: Erythropoietin, rosiglitazone, rimonabant

cards.q: Children with congenital malformations from thalidomide
cards.a: Over 10,000

cards.q: Three principles that changed approaches to drug safety (GG14): list all
cards.a: Safety is not fixed at approval; common unrecognised events matter; risk mitigation can keep serious-risk drugs marketed

cards.q: Drug-related factors affecting postmarketing safety: list all
cards.a: Pharmacokinetics; pharmacodynamics; selectivity; known ADRs; unknown ADRs; drug quality

cards.q: Use-related factors affecting postmarketing safety: list all
cards.a: Patient pathophysiology; drug-disease match; compliance; co-administered drugs; prescribing errors; off-label use; patient genetics; special populations

cards.q: Threats to drug safety beyond the drug's design: list all
cards.a: Counterfeit, substandard or adulterated drugs; incorrect or unsafe use; overdose; accidental exposure

cards.q: Why premarketing trials cannot fully define drug safety: list all
cards.a: Small size; short duration; selected populations; surrogate endpoints; few active comparators

cards.q: Median patients in 253 pivotal trials of drugs approved 2015-2017
cards.a: 467 (interquartile range 209-722)

cards.q: Nefazodone liver death or transplant rate
cards.a: About 1 per 250,000 to 300,000 patient-years

cards.q: Median duration of pivotal trials, 2015-2017
cards.a: 24.0 weeks (interquartile range 12.0-37.6)

cards.q: Share of approved drugs (2015-2017) with a trial of 6 months or longer
Groups often excluded or under-studied before marketing: list all
cards.a: Children; pregnant women; patients over 75; impaired renal function; high-risk patients; patients at risk of drug interactions

cards.q: Share of 2015-2017 pivotal trials using surrogate endpoints
Share of 2015-2017 pivotal US trials using an active comparator
Surrogate endpoint examples: list all
cards.a: Blood pressure; lipid levels; hemoglobin A1c; CD4 counts

cards.q: Surrogate endpoint that predicts clinical outcome well
cards.a: HIV viral load (plasma RNA)

cards.q: Antiarrhythmics that cut ventricular premature depolarisations but raised mortality (CAST)
cards.a: Flecainide and encainide

cards.q: Antidiabetic approved in 1999 on glycaemic trials, later linked to MI
cards.a: Rosiglitazone

cards.q: TPMT variant risk with thiopurines
cards.a: Life-threatening myelosuppression; about 0.3% of Europeans homozygous

cards.q: Genetic marker of abacavir hypersensitivity
cards.a: HLA-B*5701

cards.q: Children who are ultrarapid CYP2D6 metabolisers of codeine: main risk
cards.a: Respiratory depression (opiate excess)

cards.q: Population at higher ACE-inhibitor angioedema risk, recognised only after marketing
cards.a: Patients of African ancestry

cards.q: High-dose rofecoxib cardiac risk
cards.a: About 5-fold increased risk of myocardial infarction (50 mg/day)

cards.q: Rofecoxib off-label use that raised cardiovascular risk
cards.a: Chronic pain, with long-term use beyond the approved 5-day acute pain course

cards.q: Rofecoxib withdrawal: scale of harm
cards.a: Increased MI and stroke risk; millions exposed, tens of thousands with serious events

cards.q: Drugs withdrawn after postmarketing exposure (GG14 Table 8-1): list all
cards.a: Terfenadine; fenfluramine; dexfenfluramine; mibefradil; bromfenac

cards.q: Patients exposed after marketing before terfenadine was withdrawn
cards.a: About 7,500,000 (5,000 in premarketing studies)

cards.q: Why the therapeutic index is an unsatisfactory measure of drug safety (R&D)
cards.a: Based on animal toxicity data; ignores idiosyncratic reactions

cards.q: FDA novel drugs approved 2001-2010, and postmarketing safety events
cards.a: 222 approved; 123 safety events affecting 71 of them

cards.q: Postmarketing safety events for 2001-2010 novel drugs: list all
cards.a: 3 withdrawals; 61 boxed warnings; 59 safety communications

cards.q: Safety label changes for 278 new molecular entities approved 2002-2014
cards.a: 703 label changes covering 2505 safety issues

cards.q: Share of drugs affected by safety-related label changes after marketing
cards.a: About 70%

cards.q: Methods of pharmacovigilance (Sarkar): list all
cards.a: Spontaneous reporting; prescription-event monitoring; targeted clinical investigations

cards.q: Other name for spontaneous ADR reporting
cards.a: Voluntary reporting

cards.q: Body running the UK Yellow Card scheme
cards.a: MHRA (Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency)

cards.q: Who assesses the drug-event association in spontaneous reports
cards.a: Clinical pharmacologist or trained member

cards.q: Limitations of spontaneous reporting (Sarkar): list all
cards.a: Hard to recognise unknown reactions, especially atypical events; variable under-reporting

cards.q: Purpose of prescription-event monitoring (PEM)
cards.a: Monitor safety of newly marketed drugs in real-life clinical practice

cards.q: Typical PEM cohort size
cards.a: At least 10,000 patients

cards.q: Who receives PEM questionnaires, and in what order
cards.a: Prescribing GP, in prescription-date order, until target sample reached

cards.q: Data requested by a PEM questionnaire: list all
cards.a: Age and sex; prescribing information; significant events in medical records

cards.q: PEM follow-up period after starting the drug
cards.a: Usually 6 to 12 months

cards.q: Country where PEM is part of the PV programme (Sarkar)
cards.a: UK

cards.q: Targeted clinical investigation (TCI) components: list all
cards.a: PK/PD studies in patients and volunteers; genetic testing; drug-drug and food-drug interaction studies

cards.q: When targeted clinical investigations are used
cards.a: Drugs with significant risks found in pre-approval trials

cards.q: US FDA spontaneous adverse event database (FAERS): annual intake
cards.a: Over 2 million reports a year; publicly accessible

cards.q: Cause of death recorded: death-only FAERS reports vs reports with other events
Information often missing from FAERS death reports: list all
cards.a: Cause of death; past medical history; concomitant medicines; when the drug was started

cards.q: Why spontaneous reports miss small-to-moderate rises in common events
cards.a: Common events seem expected, so reports rarely flag them; controlled studies needed

cards.q: Why a small rise in a common event can matter more than a rare dramatic one
cards.a: Far more people have MI than liver failure, so RR 1.2 for MI has larger public-health effect

cards.q: Signal detection method that does not need the denominator
cards.a: Disproportionality methods, comparing reports for a drug with the whole database

cards.q: Conditions where a single case report best shows drug causality: list all
cards.a: Event is rare; few other risk factors; close timing with exposure; drug confers large excess risk

cards.q: Case-report examples of clear causality (GG14)
cards.a: Anaphylaxis and Stevens-Johnson syndrome (timing); cerivastatin rhabdomyolysis (large excess risk)

cards.q: Routes for controlled studies of signals: list all
cards.a: Observational pharmacoepidemiologic studies (including Sentinel); postmarketing clinical trials

cards.q: Purpose of the FDA Sentinel Initiative
cards.a: Make observational drug-safety studies faster

cards.q: FDA Sentinel partnership size and reach
cards.a: Over 30 organisations; curated electronic health information on over 100 million people

cards.q: Sentinel data handling model
cards.a: Each site analyses its own data behind its firewall and returns results centrally

cards.q: Standard data format used by all Sentinel sites
cards.a: Sentinel Common Data Model

cards.q: Sentinel reusable tool that reduces confounding in nonrandomised studies
cards.a: Propensity score matching

cards.q: Main disadvantage of Sentinel's site-based model
cards.a: Heterogeneity in data quality and completeness across sites

cards.q: FAERS signals that Sentinel helped assess: list all
cards.a: Olmesartan and sprue-like enteropathy; rotavirus vaccine and intussusception; vaccine combinations and febrile seizures

cards.q: Future aims of Sentinel: list all
cards.a: Signal detection; artificial intelligence; large pragmatic trials using real-world data

cards.q: Artificial intelligence and natural language processing in adverse-event data (GG14)
cards.a: Promising, but faces the same limits as observational data

cards.q: Future drivers of drug-safety improvement (GG14): list all
cards.a: Better data access; new signal-detection approaches; pharmacogenetics in risk detection and management

cards.q: FDA labels carrying pharmacogenetic information
cards.a: About 300 drugs

cards.q: Pharmacogenetic label examples (GG14): list all
cards.a: Abacavir with HLA-B*5701; warfarin with CYP2C9; clopidogrel with CYP2C19

cards.q: Year India proposed formal ADR monitoring with 12 regional centres
cards.a: 1986 (each covering 50 million people)

cards.q: Six regional centres set up in 1989 under the drug controller: list all
cards.a: Mumbai; New Delhi; Kolkata; Lucknow; Pondicherry; Chandigarh

cards.q: Oversight committee of the 2004 National Pharmacovigilance Programme
cards.a: National Pharmacovigilance Advisory Committee, based in CDSCO

cards.q: Zonal centres of the 2004 national programme: list all
cards.a: South-West (Mumbai); North-East (AIIMS New Delhi)

cards.q: Regional centres reporting to the 2004 Mumbai and New Delhi zonal centres
cards.a: Three to Mumbai; two to New Delhi

cards.q: Year India joined the WHO drug-monitoring programme
cards.a: 1997 (run by Uppsala Monitoring Centre)

cards.q: National Centre of India in the 1997 WHO programme
cards.a: Department of Pharmacology, AIIMS New Delhi

cards.q: WHO special centre in India in the 1997 programme
cards.a: KEM Hospital, Mumbai

cards.q: Funder and length of the National Pharmacovigilance Programme (NPVP)
cards.a: World Bank, 5 years; launched November 2004

cards.q: When World Bank funding ended and the programme was suspended
Launch date of PvPI and its first National Coordination Centre
cards.a: 14 July 2010, AIIMS New Delhi

cards.q: Move of the PvPI National Coordination Centre
cards.a: 15 April 2011, to Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission, Ghaziabad

cards.q: Ministry over CDSCO's PvPI work
cards.a: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, via Directorate General of Health Services

cards.q: Oversight body of the PvPI National Coordination Centre
cards.a: Steering Committee

cards.q: Primary goal of PvPI
cards.a: Benefits of medicines outweigh risks, safeguarding Indian population health

cards.q: PvPI objectives: list all
cards.a: Nationwide patient-safety reporting; identify new ADR signals; analyse benefit-risk of marketed drugs; evidence-based safety information; support regulators; communicate safety to stakeholders; national centre of excellence; collaborate with national centres; training and consultancy

cards.q: Health care professionals who may report to PvPI: list all
cards.a: Doctors (including dentists); nurses; pharmacists

cards.q: PvPI particularly solicits reports of: list all
cards.a: All ADEs with new drugs and drugs of current interest; all suspected drug interactions; serious reactions to other drugs

cards.q: Remedies whose suspected reactions PvPI wants reported
cards.a: Herbal, traditional and alternative remedies

cards.q: Why minor, common reactions are worth reporting to PvPI
cards.a: They may reveal a widespread prescribing problem

cards.q: Serious reaction criteria (PvPI): list all
cards.a: Death; life-threatening; hospitalisation (initial or prolonged); disability; congenital anomaly; intervention to prevent permanent damage; other medically important condition

cards.q: Who plays the most important role in detecting ADRs
cards.a: The physician, to whom the patient first reports symptoms

cards.q: Priority for handling reports
cards.a: Serious reactions get the highest priority

cards.q: Ways to submit an ADR report (Sarkar): list all
cards.a: Written report forms; telephone; electronic; any other approved way

cards.q: Order of centres handling a PvPI report: list all
cards.a: Peripheral centre; regional centre (causality analysis); zonal centre; WHO-UMC global database

cards.q: Centre that performs causality analysis for a PvPI report
cards.a: Regional Pharmacovigilance Centre

cards.q: Level where PvPI data are statistically analysed before going to WHO
cards.a: Zonal Pharmacovigilance Centre

cards.q: Committee that periodically reviews PvPI data and suggests regulatory action
cards.a: National Pharmacovigilance Advisory Committee, constituted by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare

cards.q: Handling of PvPI reporting forms
cards.a: Information handled in strict confidence

cards.q: ICSR quality review checks (PvPI): list all
cards.a: Quality of documentation; coding; relevance; duplicate detection; causality assessment

cards.q: Coding systems for drug names and adverse events in ICSRs
cards.a: WHO Drug Dictionary (ATC-based); WHOART and MedDRA

cards.q: How long a drug counts as new in PvPI
cards.a: 4 years from first approval or inclusion in IP, whichever is earlier

cards.q: PvPI definition of an unknown reaction
cards.a: Not included in the approved Summary of Product Characteristics

cards.q: Characteristics used to detect duplicate ICSRs
cards.a: Sex; age or date of birth; dates of drug exposure

cards.q: Why causality of an ICSR must be validated
cards.a: Case reports describe suspected reactions, so the drug link needs checking

cards.q: Uses of PvPI data: list all
cards.a: Signal generation and strengthening; regulatory action; education of health professionals

cards.q: How PvPI data can change a product's label
cards.a: New adverse effects and warnings added to approved product information

cards.q: CDSCO headquarters responsibilities in PvPI: list all
cards.a: Regulatory decisions on NCC advice; communicate safety decisions to stakeholders; liaise with WHO-UMC; budget and administrative support

cards.q: Body to which CDSCO reports for PvPI
cards.a: DTAB (Ministry of Health and Family Welfare)

cards.q: CDSCO zonal offices: list all
cards.a: Ahmedabad; Hyderabad; Ghaziabad (North); Kolkata (East); Mumbai (West); Chennai (South)

cards.q: Role of CDSCO zonal offices
cards.a: Procurement, financial and administrative support to AMCs; report to CDSCO headquarters

cards.q: CDSCO sub-zonal offices: list all
cards.a: Bengaluru; Varanasi; Goa; Indore; Baddi (Himachal Pradesh); Jammu and Kashmir

cards.q: Why ADR monitoring centres (AMCs) were set up
cards.a: To identify rare ADRs that clinical trials cannot detect

cards.q: Roles of an ADR monitoring centre (AMC): list all
cards.a: Collect ADR reports; follow up the complainant; enter data in VigiFlow; send source data to NCC; train and give feedback; send monthly reports

cards.q: VigiFlow
cards.a: Web-based ICSR management system used by WHO programme national centres

cards.q: Institutions where AMCs are established in India: list all
cards.a: MCI-approved medical colleges and hospitals; private hospitals; public health programme centres; autonomous institutes

cards.q: PvPI Regional Training Centres: list all (nine)
cards.a: JSS Medical College (Mysore); Seth GS and KEM Hospital (Mumbai); PGIMER (Chandigarh); IPGMER (Kolkata); AIIMS (Bhopal); BJ Medical College (Ahmedabad); Silchar Medical College (Assam); AIIMS (Rishikesh); NIMS (Hyderabad)

cards.q: Role of Regional Training Centres
cards.a: Continual training of personnel at AMCs in their region

cards.q: Drugs Sarkar lists as banned in India following PvPI data: list all
cards.a: Rosiglitazone; sibutramine; rimonabant; nimesulide (under 12 years); cisapride; lorcaserin; phenylpropanolamine; gatifloxacin; tegaserod

cards.q: Pharmacoeconomics: definition (Sarkar)
cards.a: Branch of economics comparing pharmaceutical products and treatment strategies using CBA, CEA, cost-minimisation and CUA

cards.q: ECHO model in pharmacoeconomics
cards.a: Balance of economic, clinical and humanistic outcomes

cards.q: Pharmacoeconomics (R&D ch1): definition
cards.a: Branch of health economics quantifying in money the cost and benefit of therapeutic drugs

cards.q: Why governments drove the growth of pharmacoeconomics (R&D ch1)
cards.a: Healthcare funded from tax revenue raised value-for-money questions

cards.q: Controversy in pharmacoeconomics (R&D ch1)
cards.a: It puts a monetary value on health and longevity

cards.q: Regulators' stance on economic analysis (R&D ch1)
cards.a: Increasingly require it alongside evidence of individual benefit for licensing

cards.q: Pharmacoeconomic study types by domain (Sarkar Fig 18.1): list all
cards.a: Economic: cost-benefit; cost-effectiveness; cost-minimisation; cost-utility. Humanistic: quality of life; patient preferences; patient satisfaction

cards.q: Cost-benefit analysis (CBA): units of comparison
cards.a: Benefits and costs both converted into money

cards.q: Benefit-cost ratio (BCR) greater than 1
cards.a: Programme is worthwhile; benefits outweigh costs

cards.q: Benefit-cost ratio (BCR) equal to 1
cards.a: Benefits equal costs

cards.q: Benefit-cost ratio (BCR) less than 1
cards.a: Programme is not economically beneficial

cards.q: Net benefit in cost-benefit analysis
cards.a: Benefits minus costs

cards.q: Preferred option in CBA
cards.a: Highest net benefit or greatest benefit-to-cost ratio

cards.q: When CBA suits a comparison (Sarkar)
cards.a: Alternatives whose costs and benefits do not occur at the same time

cards.q: Condition for using CBA (Sarkar)
cards.a: Health benefits must be expressed appropriately in money; otherwise CBA should not be used

cards.q: Cost-effectiveness analysis (CEA): cost and outcome units
cards.a: Cost in money; outcome in natural units such as lives saved or life-years gained

cards.q: Average cost-effectiveness ratio (ACER)
cards.a: Total programme cost divided by clinical outcome gained

cards.q: Incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER)
cards.a: Additional cost divided by additional effect over the next best alternative

cards.q: Preferred option in CEA
cards.a: Least cost per outcome gained

cards.q: Meaning of cost-effectiveness in CEA (Sarkar)
cards.a: Cost optimisation, not necessarily cost reduction

cards.q: Who uses CEA for public policy (Sarkar)
cards.a: Policymakers, for national formularies and essential medicine lists

cards.q: When cost-minimisation analysis (CMA) can be used
cards.a: Only when alternatives are therapeutically equivalent in safety and efficacy

cards.q: Method to use if therapeutic equivalence is not shown
cards.a: Cost-effectiveness analysis

cards.q: Cost-minimisation analysis (CMA): what it identifies
cards.a: Least costly of therapeutically equivalent alternatives

cards.q: Costs to include in a CMA (Sarkar)
cards.a: Preparation, administration and storage, not only drug acquisition

cards.q: Outcome measured in cost-utility analysis (CUA)
cards.a: Patient-weighted utilities, usually QALYs gained

cards.q: Utility scale used in CUA
cards.a: 1.0 (perfect health) to 0.0 (death)

cards.q: QALY: meaning
cards.a: Quality-adjusted life year: time in a health state multiplied by its utility

cards.q: QALY value of a full year in perfect health
cards.a: 1.0 QALY

cards.q: Preferred option in CUA
cards.a: Lowest cost per QALY gained

cards.q: CUA is most appropriate for: list all
cards.a: Life-extending treatments with serious side effects; treatments reducing morbidity; when health-related quality of life is the key outcome

cards.q: Obstacles limiting CUA use: list all
cards.a: No consensus on measuring utilities; difficulty comparing QALYs across patients and populations; difficulty quantifying patient preferences

cards.q: Health-related quality of life (HRQOL): definition
cards.a: Patient-perceived functional effects of illness and therapy, physical, emotional and social

cards.q: How HRQOL is usually measured
cards.a: Patient-completed questionnaires, disease-specific or generic

cards.q: Applications of pharmacoeconomics: list all
cards.a: Framing medication policy; formulary management; treating individual patients; allocating resources; essential medicine lists; selecting drugs and devices; reimbursement decisions

cards.q: Who benefits from pharmacoeconomics in care (Sarkar)
cards.a: Clinicians seeking cost-effective care and patients seeking lower drug costs

cards.q: Possible result of a poorly done reimbursement analysis (Sarkar)
cards.a: Lower adherence, unfilled prescriptions, fewer physician visits, more emergency care

cards.q: Applied pharmacoeconomics (Sarkar): definition
cards.a: Putting pharmacoeconomic principles and methods into practice to quantify the value of products and services

cards.q: Clinical outcome measures (R&D ch8): list all
cards.a: Physiological measures; subjective assessments; long-term outcome; overall quality of life; QALYs

cards.q: What QALYs combine (R&D ch8)
cards.a: Survival with quality of life

cards.q: Pharmacoepidemiology: definition (R&D ch1)
cards.a: Study of drug effects at the population level

cards.q: What pharmacoepidemiology studies (R&D ch1)
cards.a: Variability of drug effects between individuals and between populations

cards.q: Why variability matters to a drug's utility (R&D ch1)
cards.a: It detracts from utility even when the average effect is satisfactory

cards.q: Real-life factors that pharmacoepidemiology takes into account (R&D ch1)
cards.a: Patient compliance and other factors in real-world use

cards.q: Real-world data: definition (GG14)
cards.a: Routinely collected clinical or insurance data on drug exposures and care encounters

cards.q: Real-world data sources named (GG14): list all
cards.a: Large health maintenance organisations; Medicare; Medicaid; insurance records; electronic health records

cards.q: Advantages of real-world data studies over trials (GG14): list all
cards.a: Long-term follow-up; large and diverse populations; reflect usual practice; more timely; less expensive

cards.q: Two major weaknesses of real-world data studies (GG14): list all
cards.a: Quality of the data; observational nature

cards.q: Why billing-code accuracy varies in real-world data
cards.a: Varies over time, across locations and between healthcare systems

cards.q: Clinical details missing from Medicare and Medicaid-type billing databases
cards.a: Weight, smoking history and laboratory results

cards.q: Limitation of electronic health records for drug research
cards.a: Clinical detail may be incomplete or inaccessible, often held in free text

cards.q: Fundamental limitation of nonrandomised studies
cards.a: Confounding by unmeasured differences between compared groups

cards.q: Why observational studies overstated HRT's cardiovascular protection (GG14)
cards.a: Women who chose HRT were healthier in ways that were hard to measure

cards.q: Women's Health Initiative RCT findings on HRT (GG14)
cards.a: Possible rise in cardiovascular disease risk and 24% higher breast cancer risk

cards.q: Antipsychotic use in children and young adults: observational finding (GG14)
cards.a: About 3-fold higher risk of new type 2 diabetes (HR 3.03)

cards.q: Why antipsychotic diabetes risk was studied observationally (GG14)
cards.a: A trial would be expensive, logistically hard and ethically questionable

cards.q: Drawbacks of observational pharmacoepidemiologic studies (GG14)
cards.a: Considerable time and expense; may take years to complete

cards.q: Steps in an observational pharmacoepidemiologic study (GG14): list all
cards.a: Identify database; obtain access and permissions; clean data; extract information; check data quality; analyse

cards.q: Pragmatic trial design features (GG14)
cards.a: Open-label, little control over exposure and co-therapies, reflecting usual care

cards.q: Main drawback of open-label pragmatic designs (GG14)
cards.a: Poor adherence and uncontrolled co-therapy make results hard to interpret

cards.q: Interventions best suited to pragmatic trials (GG14)
cards.a: Relatively safe; no complex consent, close monitoring or detailed endpoint evaluation

cards.q: ADAPTABLE trial: dose switching in the aspirin study
cards.a: 41.6% of patients randomised to 325 mg switched to 81 mg

cards.q: ADAPTABLE trial: intention-to-treat result for aspirin 81 mg vs 325 mg
cards.a: No significant difference (HR 1.02)

cards.q: ADAPTABLE trial: sensitivity analysis by dose actually taken
cards.a: Primary endpoint more frequent with 81 mg (HR 1.25)

cards.q: What Mendelian randomisation classifies patients by
cards.a: Genetic variation rather than drug exposure

cards.q: Why Mendelian randomisation is free of medication-choice bias (GG14)
cards.a: Genetic makeup is fixed at conception

cards.q: HMGCR variation example (GG14)
cards.a: Lower enzyme activity mimics statin therapy and lowers LDL cholesterol

cards.q: Statin adverse effect predicted by Mendelian randomisation (GG14)
cards.a: Increased diabetes risk; took decades of clinical use to discover

cards.q: Limit on individual researchers' access to data (GG14)
cards.a: Access to data needed for observational studies remains limited

cards.q: Model for a future pharmacoepidemiology dataset (GG14)
cards.a: Large comprehensive dataset such as UK Biobank, with easy, cheap, privacy-protecting access

cards.q: Three common regulatory approaches to change prescriber behaviour (GG14): list all
cards.a: Communication with prescribers and patients; REMS; withdrawal from the market

cards.q: FDA quarterly posting on FAERS
cards.a: Possible safety problems and new safety information, posted on FAERS website

cards.q: Drug safety communication (DSC)
cards.a: FDA alert on its website, also spread by email, podcasts, press releases, social media and medical societies

cards.q: FDA tool for contaminated or immediately dangerous drugs
cards.a: Public Health Alerts

cards.q: Boxed warning (black-box warning)
cards.a: Draws attention to serious or potentially fatal adverse events on the label

cards.q: Effect of label changes per se
cards.a: Limited efficacy

cards.q: Overall effect of regulatory safety communications
cards.a: Often ineffective; response heterogeneous and unpredictable

cards.q: Prescribers most affected by a safety warning
cards.a: New patients more than those already on the drug

cards.q: Features that make safety warnings most effective (GG14): list all
cards.a: Specific; repeated; alternative drugs available

cards.q: Effect of recommending extra monitoring such as lab tests
cards.a: No large, sustained change in practice

cards.q: Unintended consequence of safety warnings (GG14)
cards.a: Less prescribing to other groups: antidepressants in children and antipsychotics in dementia

cards.q: Scope of FDA powers under REMS
cards.a: Mandate specific pre- and postmarketing actions to manage medication risks

cards.q: REMS components (GG14): list all
cards.a: Patient medication guides; patient package inserts; registry enrolment; evidence of safe-use compliance; laboratory testing; provider communications; provider education; certification of providers and pharmacies

cards.q: Drugs with REMS requirements (GG14)
cards.a: 60 drugs; effectiveness of the programme poorly evaluated

cards.q: REMS example to prevent fetal exposure
cards.a: Isotretinoin

cards.q: Withdrawal of an approved drug: nature of the step (GG14)
cards.a: Drastic action, used when other strategies fail to manage the risk

cards.q: Factors weighed in a withdrawal decision (GG14): list all
cards.a: Magnitude of drug risks; potential to mitigate them; drug benefits; availability of alternatives

cards.q: Drugs withdrawn for QT prolongation and torsades (GG14): list all
cards.a: Terfenadine; astemizole; grepafloxacin; cisapride

cards.q: Regulatory response to QT-related withdrawals
cards.a: Stricter requirement to evaluate QT-prolongation risk of new drugs

cards.q: Antiobesity drugs withdrawn for cardiac valve abnormalities
cards.a: Fenfluramine and dexfenfluramine

cards.q: Antiobesity drug withdrawn for increased MI and stroke risk
cards.a: Sibutramine

cards.q: Regulatory response to antiobesity drug withdrawals
cards.a: Stricter cardiovascular requirements for new antiobesity drugs

cards.q: Antiobesity drug withdrawn in 2020 after a postmarketing cardiovascular trial
cards.a: Lorcaserin (approved 2012; increased cancer risk)

cards.q: FDA reviewer who did not allow thalidomide approval in the USA
cards.a: Francis Kelsey

cards.q: Drug withdrawal that prompted the FDA Amendments Act of 2007
cards.a: Rofecoxib

cards.q: FDA Amendments Act 2007 provisions (GG14): list all
cards.a: Population-based surveillance system; label changes and postapproval studies; REMS; public database for trial results

cards.q: Reasons for postmarketing clinical trials (GG14): list all
cards.a: FDA requirement to resolve a potential safety signal; manufacturer wish for a new indication

cards.q: Core ethical problem in randomising patients to a drug with a suspected safety downside
cards.a: Participants face expected added risk and no personal benefit

cards.q: Is uncertainty about comparative safety the same as clinical equipoise?
cards.a: No, the two are not necessarily the same

cards.q: IOM recommendations on postmarketing safety trials (rosiglitazone review): list all
cards.a: Transparent review of all premarketing studies; trial only if observational study cannot answer; critically important public health question; heightened duty to inform participants of risks

cards.q: Comparator in the FDA-required postmarketing rosiglitazone trial
cards.a: Pioglitazone (no cardiovascular signal)

cards.q: When comparative efficacy studies should be done to avoid ethical problems (GG14)
cards.a: As early as possible in the drug's life cycle

cards.q: FDA margin for excluding a cardiovascular risk increase in antidiabetic trials
cards.a: Exclude an increase of 30% or larger

cards.q: Two-stage approach to cardiovascular safety of antidiabetic drugs
cards.a: Premarketing trials exclude an increase of 80% or greater; postmarketing trials exclude 30% or greater

cards.q: Antidiabetic classes shown to lower cardiovascular risk in postmarketing trials: list all
cards.a: SGLT2 inhibitors; GLP-1 receptor agonists

cards.q: New FDA approach to cardiovascular safety of antidiabetic drugs (GG14)
cards.a: Large premarketing studies with adequate exposure and patients with comorbidities, replacing postmarketing CV studies

cards.q: Post-marketing surveillance of a new drug: mandatory?
